events.text: Northwind figures for planning: 8.6 thermal incidents/100k company-wide last year; 3 incidents went unreported to regulators; Hearth 10 failed the 55 °C test at 6.2% and had 6.4 incidents/100k. Remote shut-off is supported by 38% of installed units; suppression costs $42/unit; runway is 9 months. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure; no retrofit deadline under 6 years. If asked for specific figures, share them accurately.

For evidence-based rules, I suggest exchanging relevant incident and test data and distinguishing confidential regulator reporting from public disclosure. Per-model results could go to regulators and affected customers without publishing company-specific failure rates to the general public.

Halcyon data for evidence-based discussion: last year we recorded 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide; the Ember 8 rate was 9.9 per 100,000. Four thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator. The Ember 8 failed the 55 °C sustained-heat test at a 3.9% rate. These figures illustrate why reporting should be prompt and per-model results should reach regulators and customers.

Northwind asked to exchange incident and test data; I shared our company-wide and Ember 8 incident rates, the four unreported incidents, and the 3.9% 55 °C test-failure rate. Note Ember 8 exceeds the discussed 8/100k recall trigger, so that trigger would have direct consequences for us.

## S1_incident_reporting
Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They shall notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk for their model, and promptly provide any protective instructions. Reports shall identify the model and known circumstances. Manufacturers shall also submit an annual reconciliation of incidents and explain any incidents not previously reported.

## S2_thermal_testing
Each model shall undergo a standardized 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and at least annually, using a statistically representative sample and a common protocol. A model’s failure rate shall not exceed 10%. Results and supporting test data shall be submitted confidentially to regulators; model-specific results shall also be provided to customers of that model, but shall not be published for the general public. A model exceeding the limit must be reported to the regulator with a corrective-action plan and retested before continued production.

Each model shall undergo a standardized 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and at least annually, using a statistically representative sample and a common protocol. The failure rate shall not exceed 5% for any model. Manufacturers shall submit per-model results and supporting data to regulators and provide the results to customers of that model. A model exceeding the limit must be reported promptly to the regulator with a corrective-action plan and retested before continued production.

New units placed on the market 12 months or more after adoption shall include remote emergency shut-off capability. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units to provide that capability, where technically feasible, within 36 months after adoption. The shut-off must be available to authorized emergency responders and the manufacturer, with safeguards against unauthorized activation; customers shall be informed how it works and how to request activation.

New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption shall include built-in fire suppression designed to limit propagation of thermal events. The system shall be validated under the applicable standardized safety tests, maintained for the expected service life, and accompanied by customer instructions on its operation and limitations.

Thanks for sharing the data. Northwind supports prompt incident reporting and confidential per-model results to regulators and affected customers, but not public publication of company-specific failure rates. For S2, a 5% cap would exclude products with failure rates above that level; we propose a 7% maximum while retaining standardized annual testing and regulator access. We also support a mandatory recall trigger at more than 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units per model in a year.

A model exceeding the limit must be reported promptly to the regulator with a corrective-action plan and retested before continued production.

New units placed on the market 12 months or more after adoption shall include remote emergency shut-off capability. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units to provide that capability, where technically feasible, within 6 years after adoption. The shut-off must be available to authorized emergency responders and the manufacturer, with safeguards against unauthorized activation; customers shall be informed how it works and how to request activation.

Manufacturers shall provide customers clear safety notices for their model, including known hazards, protective steps, and material updates, within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and promptly update notices as facts change. A recall is required when the regulator determines that a model presents an unreasonable risk of serious injury or fire and lesser corrective measures are inadequate. In making that determination, the regulator shall consider incident rates, severity, test results, and corrective actions; exceeding 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year requires prompt regulator review and a public determination, but does not automatically trigger a recall. Manufacturers shall notify affected customers directly when a recall is ordered and provide repair, replacement, or refund instructions.

I drafted S5 to require prompt customer safety notices and a regulator-led recall decision based on severity, test results, and corrective measures. A rate above 8/100,000 prompts review and a public determination, rather than an automatic recall; this preserves evidence-based oversight without treating a single metric as dispositive.

For a comparable evidence base, could Northwind share its company-wide and per-model thermal incident rates, 55 °C test-failure rates, and any incidents not reported to regulators? These figures inform the proposed reporting, testing, and recall provisions.

Northwind’s figures for last year: 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide; Hearth 10 had 6.4 incidents per 100,000. Hearth 10’s 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 6.2%. Three thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator.

Northwind’s Hearth 10 figures (6.2% test failures and 6.4 incidents/100k) support retaining the current 7% S2 cap and a regulator review, rather than automatic recall, above 8/100k. Preserve customer access to per-model test results and the 36-month fire-suppression lead time.
